- `grouper` – the item that was grouped by (e.g., the string `"India"` or `"Japan"`).  
- `list` – a list of all items in this group (e.g., a list of all cities with `country='India'`).  

### The `@ifchanged` directive

The `@ifchanged` directive in PyBlade is used **only inside loops** and helps you detect when a value changes between iterations. You might find it very useful to conditionally render content based on whether a variable has changed compared to its previous state.  

When used without arguments, `@ifchanged` checks its own rendered contents against its previous state and only displays the content if it has changed.  For example, this displays a list of days, only displaying the month if it changes:

```html
<h1>Archive for {{ year }}</h1>

@for (date in dates)
    @ifchanged
        <h3>{{ date.strftime('%B') }}</h3>
    @endifchanged
    <a href="/{{ date.strftime('%m/%d').lower() }}">{{ date.strftime('%d') }}</a>
@endfor
```

If given one or more variables as arguments to `@ifchanged` directive, it checks whether any variable has changed. For example, the following shows the date every time it changes, while showing the hour if either the hour or the date has changed:

```html
@for (date in dates)
    @ifchanged (date.date)
        <strong>{{ date.date }}</strong>
    @endifchanged
    
    @ifchanged (date.hour, date.date)
        <span>{{ date.hour }}</span>
    @endifchanged
@endfor
```

You can use an `@else` clause inside `@ifchanged` to define an alternative output when the value has **not** changed. For example, the following alternates between `red` and `blue` colors when `ballot_id` changes, otherwise uses `gray`:  

```html
@for (match in matches)
    <div style="background-color:
        @ifchanged(match.ballot_id)
            @cycle('red', 'blue')
        @else
            gray
        @endifchanged
    ">
        {{ match }}
    </div>
@endfor
```

### Capturing the present with `@now`

The `@now` directive is used to display the current date and time in a template. It takes a string format time based on Python’s standard [datetime module syntax](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#strftime-strptime-behavior).  

For example, if you want to show the full date and time, you can write:  

```html
It is @now("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
```

If the current date and time is March 12, 2025, at 14:30:45, the output will be:  

```
It is 2025-03-12 14:30:45
```

Sometimes, you may need to store the output of `@now` in a variable to reuse it in different parts of the template. This can be done using the `as` keyword.  

```html
@now("%B" as current_month)

@if (current_month == "December")
    <p>Happy holidays! It's {{ current_month }}, the festive season.</p>
@else
    <p>Welcome to {{ current_month }}! Hope you have a great month.</p>
@endif
```

> **Note**
>
> When the `as` keyword is used within the `@now` directive to store the current date and time in a variable, the directive does not produce any output on that line.

The table below outlines some of the most commonly used  datetime format specifiers from Python’s `datetime` module:  

| Format  | Description               | Example Output (March 12, 2025, 14:30:45) |
|---------|---------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `%Y`    | Full year                  | `2025`                                   |
| `%y`    | Short year (last two digits) | `25`                                  |
| `%m`    | Month (zero-padded)         | `03`                                   |
| `%B`    | Full month name             | `March`                                |
| `%b`    | Short month name            | `Mar`                                  |
| `%d`    | Day (zero-padded)           | `12`                                   |
| `%A`    | Full weekday name           | `Wednesday`                            |
| `%a`    | Short weekday name          | `Wed`                                  |
| `%H`    | Hour (24-hour format)       | `14`                                   |
| `%I`    | Hour (12-hour format)       | `02`                                   |
| `%M`    | Minutes                     | `30`                                   |
| `%S`    | Seconds                     | `45`                                   |
| `%p`    | AM/PM                       | `PM`                                   |

## URLs and static files

### Generating URLs with `@url`

The `@url` directive generates an absolute path (a URL without the domain name) based on a named route and optional parameters. Any special characters in the resulting URL are automatically encoded.  

To generate a URL, pass the route name as the first argument, followed by any required parameters. The parameters should be comma-separated.  

```html
<a href="@url('some-url-name', post.id, post.slug)">Read the post</a>
```

In this example, the generated URL will dynamically include the values of `post.id` and `post.slug` in the appropriate placeholders defined in the url pattern configuration.  

Instead of positional arguments, keyword arguments can be used for better clarity:  

```html
<a href="@url('some-url-name', pk=product.id)">Show product</a>
```

> **Warning**
>
> It is important to note that positional and keyword arguments cannot be mixed within the same `@url` directive. Additionally, all required parameters must be provided to avoid errors.

**Example with dynamic route in Django**

Consider a view function `client()` inside the `views.py` file, which requires a client ID as a parameter. Its corresponding route might look like this:  

```python title="urls.py"
path("client/<int:id>/", views.client, name="client-detail")
``` 

The correct way to generate a link in a template would be:  

```html
<a href="@url('client-detail', client.id)">View Client</a>
```

If `client.id` is `123`, the generated URL would be:  

```text
/client/123/
```

> **Warning**
>
> If the **URL** you’re reversing doesn’t exist, you’ll get an `NoReverseMatch` exception raised, which will cause your site to display an error page.
 

When working with Django, if you’d like to retrieve a namespaced URL, specify the fully qualified name:

```html
<a href="@url('myapp:view-name')">Visit MyApp</a>
```
This will follow the normal namespaced URL resolution strategy, including using any hints provided by the context as to the current application. 

### Marking the current page with `@active`

`@active` renders its content while the reader is on the page it names, and is closed with `@endactive`. It is what a navigation menu needs to mark where the reader is.

```html
@active ('dashboard')
    <span>You are on the dashboard.</span>
@endactive
```

The most common use is applying a class to the element wrapping a link. Because `@active` renders whatever is inside it, that class goes in the block:

```html
<li class="@active('dashboard')active@endactive">
    <a href="@url('dashboard')">Dashboard</a>
</li>
<li class="@active('profile')active@endactive">
    <a href="@url('profile')">Profile</a>
</li>
```

If the reader is on the dashboard, the first `<li>` is rendered with `class="active"` and the second with an empty class.

#### Naming the page

What you pass names the page in one of two ways. A plain name is the name of the route, as Django resolved it; anything starting with `/` is matched against the path instead. Either form accepts `*`, standing for anything.

| What you write | What it matches |
| -------------- | --------------- |
| `'dashboard'` | The route named `dashboard`. |
| `'blog:index'` | The `index` route of the `blog` namespace. |
| `'index'` | The same route, named without its namespace. |
| `'blog:*'` | Every route in the `blog` namespace. |
| `'/posts/'` | That exact path, and no other. |
| `'/posts/*'` | `/posts/`, `/posts/3`, `/posts/3/edit`, and anything else beneath it. |

The last one is what the parent of a menu needs, so that it stays marked while the reader is on any page below it:

```html
@active ('/posts/*')
    <span>Somewhere in the posts.</span>
@endactive
```

You can name several pages at once, and the block is rendered if the reader is on any of them:

```html
@active ('posts', '/archive/*')
    <span>Somewhere in the writing.</span>
@endactive
```

#### Showing something else instead

Like `@if`, `@active` takes an `@else` for when the reader is somewhere else:

```html
@active ('dashboard')
    <span>You are here.</span>
@else
    <a href="@url('dashboard')">Go to the dashboard</a>
@endactive
```

> **Note: Inside a persisted element, use pb:current**
>
> `@active` is resolved when the server renders the page. An element kept across page loads with `@persist` is not re-rendered, so a link inside one should use the [`pb:current`](/live-components/features/navigation#highlighting-active-links) directive instead, which the browser applies after each navigation.

### The `@querystring` directive 

PyBlade provides an intuitive way to generate and manipulate query strings dynamically. 

The `@querystring` directive constructs a URL-encoded query string by adding or modifying parameters in the current query string.

```html
@querystring(color="green", size="M")
```

Each keyword argument will be added to the current query string, replacing any existing value for that key. For instance, if the currrent query string is `?color=red`, The above code would output :

```text
?color=green&size=M
```

Setting a query parameter to `None` will remove it from the query string.  

If a parameter is a list, `@querystring` will generate multiple key-value pairs, maintaining the structure.  

```html
@querystring(color=my_list)
```

If `my_list = ["red", "blue"]`, the output will be:  

```text
?color=red&color=blue
```

> **Note**
>
> If no parameters are provided, the `querystring` directive outputs the current query string verbatim exactly as it appears in the request, or a leading `?` if the query string is empty.

A common example of using this directive is to preserve the current query string when displaying a page of paginated results, while adding a link to the next and previous pages of results. For example, if the paginator is currently on page `3`, and the current query string is `?color=blue&size=M&page=3`, the following code :

```html
@querystring(page=page.next_page_number)
```

... would output:

```text
?color=blue&size=M&page=4
```

For efficiency, you may also store the generated query string in a variable for reuse:  

```html
@querystring(page=page.next_page_number as next_page)
```

Then use it multiple times in your template:  

```html
<a href="/products/{{ next_page }}">Next Page</a>
```

### The `@static` directive

In PyBlade, the `@static` directive provides a convenient way to link to static files such as images, stylesheets, JavaScript files, and other resources that are served from a **static** folder.  

To link to a static file, use the `@static` directive with the path to the file. This will generate the appropriate URL for the static resource. The format of the URL is typically determined by the project's static settings.  

```html
<img src="@static('images/hi.jpg')" alt="Hi!">
```

This will resolve to the appropriate URL for the image, ensuring it is properly linked according to your static file configuration.  

You can also pass context variables to the `@static` directive. For example, if you have a `user_stylesheet` variable passed from the view, you can use it to dynamically link to a user's custom stylesheet:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="@static(user_stylesheet)" media="screen">
```

This way, the value of `user_stylesheet` will be treated as the path to the stylesheet, which can be modified based on the current user’s preferences or other dynamic conditions.  

Sometimes, you may want to retrieve a static URL without displaying it immediately. You may store the URL in a variable for later use. You can do this by using the `as` keyword, similar to other directives that assign values:

```html
@static('images/hi.jpg' as my_photo)
<img src="{{ my_photo }}">
```

This stores the static URL for the image in the `my_photo` variable, which you can then use anywhere in the template.  

#### The `@get_static_prefix` directive

If you need more control over how the static URL is injected into the template, you can use the `@get_static_prefix` directive. This will give you the static URL prefix, which is typically the base URL for static files.  

```html
<img src="@get_static_prefix images/hi.jpg" alt="Hi!">
```

This allows you to explicitly append the path to the static resource to the URL prefix.  

Alternatively, you can store the static prefix in a variable to avoid repeated processing of the same value:

```html
@get_static_prefix(as STATIC_PREFIX)
<img src="{{ STATIC_PREFIX }}images/hi.jpg" alt="Hi!">
<img src="{{ STATIC_PREFIX }}images/hi2.jpg" alt="Hello!">
```

By doing this, the static prefix is stored in the `STATIC_PREFIX` variable, making it easier to use the same prefix multiple times throughout the template.  

####  The `@get_media_prefix` directive

Similar to `@get_static_prefix`, the `@get_media_prefix` directive provides the media URL prefix. This is useful when you need to link to media files, which are typically served separately from static files.  

For example, you can use `@get_media_prefix` to set a data attribute for media URLs:

```html
<body data-media-url="@get_media_prefix">
```

## Internationalization in templates

Internationalization within PyBlade templates are performed by the use of two directives and a slightly different syntax than in Python code to translate some parts of rendered text. 

> **Warning**
>
> Translated strings will not be escaped when rendered in a template. This allows you to include HTML in translations, for example for emphasis, but potentially dangerous characters (e.g., `"` ) will also be rendered unchanged.

### The `@translate` directive

The `@translate` directive allows you to translate either a constant string (enclosed in single or double quotes) or variable content:

```html
<title>@translate("This is the title.")</title>
<title>@translate(myvar)</title>
```

If the `noop` option is present, variable lookup still takes place but the translation is skipped. This is useful when "stubbing out" content that will require translation in the future:

```html
<title>@translate("myvar", noop=True)</title>
```

> **Note**
>
> It’s not possible to mix a template variable inside a string within `@translate`. If your translations require strings with variables (placeholders), use [`@blocktranslate`](#the-blocktranslate-directive) instead.

If you’d like to retrieve a translated string without displaying it, you can use the following syntax:

```html
@translate("This is the title" as the_title)

<title>{{ the_title }}</title>
<meta name="description" content="{{ the_title }}">
```

In practice, you’ll use this to get a string you can use in multiple places in a template or so you can use the output as an argument for other PyBlade directives:

```html
@translate("starting point as start)
@translate("end point" as end)
@translate("La Grande Boucle" as race)

<h1>
  <a href="/" title="@blocktranslate Back to '{{ race }}' homepage @endblocktranslate">{{ race }}</a>
</h1>
<p>
    
@for (stage in tour_stages)
    @cycle(start, end): {{ stage }}@if (loop.index % 2 == 0)<br>@else, @endif
@endfor
</p>
```

The `@translate` directive also supports contextual markers using the `context` keyword argument:

```html
@translate("May", context="month name")
```

> **Note: Pro tip**
>
> You may use the `@trans` directive which is a shorthand of the `@translate` directive.

### The `@blocktranslate` directive

Unlike `@translate`, the `@blocktranslate` directive allows marking complex sentences that include both literals and variable content by using placeholders:

```html
@blocktranslate
    This string will have {{ value }} inside.
@endblocktranslate
```

To translate a template expression, such as accessing object attributes or calling object methods, bind the expression to a local variable within the translation block:

```html
@blocktranslate(amount=article.price)
    That will cost $ {{ amount }}.
@endblocktranslate
```

You can use multiple expressions inside a single `@blocktranslate`:

```html
@blocktranslate(book_t=book.title, author_t=author.title() )
    This is {{ book_t }} by {{ author_t }}.
@endblocktranslate
```

If resolving a block argument fails, `@blocktranslate` falls back to the default language by temporarily deactivating the current language.

> **Warning**
>
> Other PyBlade directives like `@for` or `@if` are **not** allowed inside `@blocktranslate`.

### Pluralization in `@blocktranslate`

To use pluralization:

1. Bind a counter variable as `counter`.
2. Specify both singular and plural forms using the `@plural` directive.

Example:

```html
@blocktranslate(counter=list.length)
    There is only one {{ name }} object.
@plural
    There are {{ counter }} {{ name }} objects.
@endblocktranslate
```

A more complex example:

```html
@blocktranslate(amount=article.price, counter=i.length)
    That will cost $ {{ amount }} per year.
@plural
    That will cost $ {{ amount }} per {{ counter }} years.
@endblocktranslate
```

If the `counter` variable stores a number greater than `1`, the singular form will be translated, otherwise, the pluram form will be translated.

> **Warning**
>
> It is important to call this counter variable `counter`.

You can retrieve a translated string without displaying it:

```html
@blocktranslate(as the_title)
    The title is {{ the_title }}.
@endblocktranslate

<title>{{ the_title }}</title>
<meta name="description" content="{{ the_title }}">
```
The `@blocktranslate` directive also supports contextual markers using the `context` keyword argument:

```html
@blocktranslate(name=user.username, context="greeting")
    Hi {{ name }}
@endblocktranslate
```

The `trimmed` argument can be used to remove unnecessary whitespace and newlines:

```html
@blocktranslate(trimmed=True)
    First sentence.
    Second paragraph.
@endblocktranslate()
```

In `.po` files, this results in
```text
"First sentence. Second paragraph."
```

 rather than:

```text
"\n  First sentence.\n  Second paragraph.\n"
```

### Generating translation files
PyBlade provides CLI commands to help you manage translation files for your internationalized templates.

To generate translation files for a specific locale, use the `pyblade make:messages` command with the `--locale` argument:

```bash
pyblade make:messages --locale fr
```

Or using the short form:

```bash
pyblade make:messages -l fr
```

This command will scan your templates for translatable strings and create or update `.po` files for the specified locale.

### Compiling translation files

After translating the strings in your `.po` files, you need to compile them into `.mo` files for use in your application. Use the `pyblade messages:compile` command:

```bash
pyblade messages:compile
```

This command compiles all `.po` files into their corresponding `.mo` files, making the translations available to your application.

### Other translation utilities

PyBlade also provides a few small utilities that can be useful when working with translations.

#### `@lang`

The `@lang` directive gives you the **current language code**. You can store it in a template variable and use it wherever you need it.

A common use case is setting the `lang` attribute of your HTML document:

```html

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="@lang">
<head>
...
</head>
<body>
...
</body>
</html>
```

If the current language is `en-us`, PyBlade renders:

```html
<html lang="en-us">
```

You can also use the language code anywhere else in your template:

```html
<p>Current language: @lang</p>
```

#### `@languages`

The `@languages` directive gives you the languages configured for your application. This is particularly useful when building a language selector.

```html
@lang(as CURRENT_LANGUAGE)
@languages(as LANGUAGES)

<select name="language">
    @for (language in LANGUAGES)
    <option value="{{ language.code }}" @selected(language.code == CURRENT_LANGUAGE)>
    {{ language.name }}
    </option>
    @endfor
</select>
```

Each language provides information such as its `code` and display `name`. The exact languages available depend on your application's translation configuration.

This keeps language selection framework-agnostic: whether your application uses Django, Flask, Quart, or another supported framework, `@languages` provides the same PyBlade interface.

> **Note: Django projects**
>
> In Django projects, if the `django.template.context_processors.i18n` context processor is enabled, Django already provides `LANGUAGE_CODE`, `LANGUAGES`, and `LANGUAGE_BIDI` in the template context.
>
> You can therefore access them directly without using `@lang` or `@languages`.


---

# Components

URL: https://docs.pyblade.com/components

As your application grows, you will often have UI elements that appear in many places: buttons, cards, alerts, navigation items, and more.

You could create these elements as partials and include them wherever needed. However, some UI elements also need their own data, configuration, or behavior. This is where **components** become useful.

Instead of writing the same HTML again and again, PyBlade components let you define a reusable piece of UI once and use it throughout your application with a simple, consistent syntax.

Let's see how to create components, pass data to them, and customize their content.

## Creating a component

A component is simply a `.html` file that can be created manually, but for convenience, PyBlade provides the `pyblade make:component` command to generate a new component automatically.

By default, components must be stored inside the `components` folder, located within your project root directory:

```text
my_project/
  components/
    alert.html
    card.html
    ...
  static/
  templates/
  pyblade.toml
```

You can manually create a component inside the `components` folder, or use the provided command to generate one:

```bash
pyblade make:component alert
```

This command will create the file: `components/alert.html`
```text
components/
  alert.html
```

> **Warning**
>
> It is important to avoid naming your component `slot`, as this could lead to conflicts with PyBlade's built-in `pb-slot` tag used for creating new [slots](#slots). Rendering a component named `slot` will interfere with the `slot` system, causing potential issues.

## Where components are found

PyBlade looks for a component in your project's `components/` folder (the folder set by [`paths.components`](/configuration#paths)).

In a **Django** project, an app can bring components of its own, in a `components/` folder inside the app, next to its `templates/`. They are found after the project's, in the order your apps are listed in `INSTALLED_APPS`:

```text
components/badge.html              # 1. the project's own
apps/billing/components/badge.html # 2. then each app's
```

This means:

- an app's components need nothing to be registered: if the app is installed, its components can be used from every template, with the same syntax as the project's,
- the project can **replace** a component an app provides by writing one with the same name in its own `components/` folder,
- live components work the same way, and a live component keeps its template next to its class, wherever it is.

`pyblade make:component --app billing` creates a component in an app. See [creating files in a Django app](/cli/commands#creating-files-in-a-django-app).

## Rendering components

The **preferred way** to include a component in your template is by using a **PyBlade component tag**. Component tags start with `pb-`, followed by the component file name without extension.

For example, if you have a component file named `alert.html`, you can include it in your template like this:

```html
<pb-alert />
```

Similarly, for a `user-profile.html` or `user_profile.html` component, you would write:

```html
<pb-user-profile />
```

A PyBlade component tag can be **self-closing** — when the component does not need any inner content:

```html
<pb-alert />
```

or **paired** — when you need to include content inside the component:

```html
<pb-alert>
    This is an important message!
</pb-alert>
```

### The `@component` directive

PyBlade also provides an alternative way to render components using the `@component` directive:

```
@component("alert")
```

```
@component("user-profile")
```

While this method works, **it is not as intuitive as using component tags**. The tag-based syntax is visually clearer and aligns with HTML syntax.

### Handling nested components

If your components are stored inside subdirectories within `components/`, you can indicate this hierarchy using a **dot notation** in both approaches.

For instance, if you have a component file located at `components/forms/dropdown.html`, you can render it as follows:

```html
<pb-forms.dropdown />
```

or, alternatively:

```
@component('forms.dropdown')
```

## Passing data to components

When creating a component, it often expects certain values (variables) to be passed in when used.
You can pass data to PyBlade components using HTML attributes. Hard-coded, primitive values may be passed to the component using simple HTML attribute strings. Python expressions and variables should be passed to the component via attributes that use the `:` character as a prefix.

If you're using the `@component` directive to render a component, you may pass data as the second parameter, in the form of python a dictionary.

To make it clear, let's assume we have the following component:

```html title="components/alert.html"
<div class="alert alert-{{ type }}">
    {{ message }}
</div>
```

As you can see, the component is waiting for two variables: `type` and `message`. We can provide them in the template where we want to use it like this:

```html title="templates/home.html"
<pb-alert type="success" message="Operation completed successfully."/>
```

or:

```html title="templates/home.html"
@component('alert', {'type':'success', 'message':'Operation completed successfully.'})
```

The rendered output will look like this:

```html
<div class="alert alert-success">
    Operation completed successfully.
</div>
```

### Regular vs Bound attributes

When using PyBlade's component tags (`<pb-component-name>`), you can pass data as *Regular HTML attributes* (without `:`) or *Bound attributes* (starting with `:`).
Both methods serve different purposes in how data is interpreted and passed to the component.

#### Regular attributes

Regular attributes are passed as **static strings**. These values are not evaluated as Python expressions but are used as they are.

For example:

```html
<pb-alert type="success" message="Operation completed successfully." />
```

Here, `"success"` and `"Operation completed successfully."` are passed as plain strings. The component receives them as-is, without any evaluation.

#### Bound Attributes

When an attribute starts with `:`, it is treated as a **Python expression**, meaning it is evaluated before being passed to the component.

For example, assuming we have a variable `status` with a dynamic string value, we may pass it to the component by prefixing it with the `:` character like this:

```html
<pb-alert :type="status" message="Operation done." />
```

In this example, `:type="status"` passes the **value of `status`** instead of the string `"status"`.

## The `@props` Directive

The `@props` directive in PyBlade allows you to define default values for properties (variables) within a component. This is particularly useful when creating reusable components where some properties might be optional. If a value is not provided when the component is used, it will automatically fallback to the default value specified in the `@props` directive.

The `@props` directive accepts a dictionary where the `keys` represent the names of the properties (variables) that the component expects, while the `values` represent the default values that will be used if no explicit value is provided when using the component.

For example, consider the following **alert** component:

```html title="components/alert.html"
@props({'type':'info', 'message':'Default message'})

<div class="alert alert-{{ type }}">
    {{ message }}
</div>
```

When using this `alert` component, you can either pass a custom `type` and `message` attributes, or let the component fall back to its default values.

```html title="templates/home.html"
<pb-alert message="User created successfully" />
```

Here, only the `message` property is provided as an attribute with the value `"User created successfully"`, but the `type` is omitted. Because of this, the default value of `type` (`"info"`) will be used.

The final rendered HTML will look like this:

```html
<div class="alert alert-info">
    User created successfully
</div>
```

Since only `message` was specified, only the message text changed, but the type remains `info` resulting in the class name `alert-info` being applied.

## Component attributes

We've already discussed passing declared data (props) to a component. But sometimes the caller needs to pass **extra HTML attributes** — like `class`, `id`, `data-*`, `type`, `href` — that aren't part of the component's declared props, but that should still land on the component's root element.

Any attribute passed on a component tag that isn't consumed by `@props` (or an expected variable) is automatically collected into a variable called `attributes`, available inside the component. Write it directly on the root element to apply all of it at once:

```html title="components/card.html"
<div {{ attributes }}>
    <!-- Component content -->
</div>
```

For example, if you render:

```html title="templates/home.html"
<pb-card class="mt-4" :user="user"/>
```

the `class="mt-4"` attribute isn't declared anywhere by the component, so it flows straight into `attributes` and gets printed on the root `<div>`.

`attributes` behaves like a plain, dict-like collection of whatever extra attributes were passed — you interact with it the same way you'd interact with any HTML attribute or any Python mapping.

### Default values and automatic merging

Declare the attribute the way you normally would in HTML, alongside `{{ attributes }}`, and PyBlade treats your literal value as the **default**, merging or overriding it with whatever the caller passed — depending on the attribute.

```html title="components/card.html"
<div class="card-item rounded-full" {{ attributes }}>
    {{ user.name }}
</div>
```

If you use the component like this:

```html title="templates/home.html"
<pb-card class="mb-4" :user="user"/>
```

The final HTML rendered will be:

```html
<div class="card-item rounded-full mb-4">
    <!-- Contents of the message variable -->
</div>
```

You wrote `class="..."` exactly like you would on any HTML element, and PyBlade combined it with the caller's `class` automatically.

### Why `class` is special

`class` always **combines** rather than replaces, because that's what you almost always want with CSS classes: the component's base styling stays, and the caller's classes are appended. This happens automatically any time a literal `class` attribute sits on the same tag as `{{ attributes }}`.

### Non-class attributes

For every other attribute, your literal value is a genuine default: the caller's value wins if they passed one, otherwise your literal stays as-is.

```html title="components/button.html"
<button type="button" {{ attributes }}>
    Click Me
</button>
```

If you use the component as follows:

```html title="templates/form.html"
<pb-button type="submit" />
```

The rendered HTML will be:

```html
<button type="submit">
    Click Me
</button>
```

Had the caller not passed `type` at all, the button would have kept `type="button"`.

### Reading a specific attribute

Since `attributes` is a mapping, read a value the same way you'd read any attribute or dict entry:

```html
{{ attributes.class }}
```

Fall back to a default the same way you would with any Python value:

```html
{{ attributes.class or 'default-class' }}
```

For attribute names that aren't valid Python identifiers (containing `-`, `:`, etc.), use item access instead of dot access:

```html
{{ attributes['data-toggle'] }}
```

## Slots

Props let you pass **data** to a component, such as strings, numbers, or booleans. But sometimes you want to pass **content** instead: a paragraph, an icon, a button, or even a whole block of HTML. That's what **slots** are for.

Think of a component as a template with one or more spaces that the caller can fill with content. The component decides where these spaces appear and what surrounds them, while the caller provides what goes inside.

Inside the component, each space is accessed through a variable: `slot` for the main, unnamed content, or a custom name for additional slots. When using the component, the caller fills these slots by placing content between the component's opening and closing tags.

### The default slot

Let's imagine a `card` component with the following template:

```html title="components/card.html"
<div class="card">
    <h2>{{ title }}</h2>

    <div class="card-content">
        {{ slot }}
    </div>
</div>
```

Here, `{{ slot }}` is the component's default, unnamed slot. It represents the content provided by whoever uses the component.

You fill the default slot by placing content between the component's opening and closing tags:

```html title="templates/index.html"
<pb-card title="Welcome">
    <p>This is the content of the card.</p>
</pb-card>
```

Everything between `<pb-card>` and `</pb-card>` becomes the value of `slot` inside the component. PyBlade then renders that content wherever `{{ slot }}` appears in the component template.

> **Warning**
>
> The `slot` variable is **not escaped by default** because it is intended to contain rendered HTML. Only use slots with trusted or properly sanitized content. Passing untrusted user input directly into a slot can introduce **cross-site scripting (XSS)** vulnerabilities.

### Named slots

A component can have more than one slot when it needs to accept different pieces of content.

For example, we can give our `alert` component a named `title` slot in addition to its default slot:

```html title="components/alert.html"
<div class="alert alert-{{ type }}">
    <h2>{{ title }}</h2>
    
    <div>
        {{ slot }}
    </div>
</div>
```

The `title` variable represents the named slot, while `slot` remains the default, unnamed slot.

To fill a named slot, use the `<pb-slot>` tag with the corresponding `name` attribute:

```html title="templates/home.html"
<pb-alert type="danger">
    <pb-slot name="title">Server Error</pb-slot> <!-- [!code highlight] -->

    <strong>Whoops!</strong> Something went wrong!
</pb-alert>
```

The content inside `<pb-slot name="title">` is assigned to the `title` slot. Any content outside an explicit `<pb-slot>` remains part of the default `slot`.

The result is:

```html
<div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h2>Server Error</h2>
    
    <div>
        <strong>Whoops!</strong> Something went wrong!
    </div>
</div>
```

> **Tip: Pro Tip**
>
> You can use the shorthand syntax `<pb-slot:title> ... </pb-slot>` instead of `<pb-slot name="title"> ... </pb-slot>` when defining a named slot.


---

# Template Inheritence

URL: https://docs.pyblade.com/template-inheritence

Most web applications have a common structure shared by many pages, such as a navigation bar, a header, a footer, and a main content area.

Repeating this structure in every template makes your code harder to maintain. If you need to change the navigation, for example, you would have to update every page that contains it.

PyBlade lets you define this shared structure once as a base **layout**. You can define a shared layout once and let your other templates extend it, keeping the common structure in one place while each page provides its own content.

This is called **template inheritance**.
## Defining a Layout

A layout is a reusable template that provides the common structure shared by multiple pages. Other templates can then inherit this layout and provide the content specific to each page.

Let's start with a simple base layout:

```html title="templates/layouts/base.html" lineNumbers
<html>
    <head>
        <title>My App - {{ title }}</title>
    </head>

    <body>
        <header>
            <h1>Welcome to My App</h1>
        </header>

        <aside>
            ...
        </aside>

        <main>
            @block("content")
                <p>Nothing to display yet.</p>
            @endblock
        </main>

        <footer>
            &copy; @now('%Y') - My App
        </footer>
    </body>
</html>
```

The important part here is the `@block` directive. A block defines a named area of the layout that child templates can replace.

In this example, `content` has some default content. If a child template does not provide its own `content` block, this default content will be displayed.

You can define as many blocks as your layout needs:

```html
@block("header")
    <h1>Welcome to My App</h1>
@endblock

@block("content")
    <p>Nothing to display yet.</p>
@endblock
```

We'll see how child templates override these blocks in the next section.

You'll also notice the `title` variable in the `<title>` element. Rather than making the page title a block, we'll use a **named slot** so that each child template can provide its own title.

## Extending a Layout

Once you have a layout, a child template can inherit it using the `@extends` directive:

```html title="templates/home.html" lineNumbers
@extends("layouts.base")
```

The value passed to `@extends` uses **dot notation** to identify the layout file. So `layouts.base` refers to `templates/layouts/base.html`.

PyBlade also supports regular file paths, meaning you could write `@extends("layouts/base.html")` instead.

After extending a layout, the child template can provide content for the blocks defined by the parent. Child templates use the `@block` directive to override a block:

```html title="templates/home.html" lineNumbers
@extends("layouts.base")

<pb-slot name="title">Home</pb-slot>

@block("content")
    <p>Welcome to the home page!</p>
@endblock
```

When PyBlade renders this template, the content of `@block("content")` replaces the corresponding `@block("content")` in the parent layout.

If the parent defined default content for that block, the child's block replaces it completely.

### Adding to existing content

Sometimes you don't want to completely replace the content provided by the parent. You may want to keep it and add something of your own.

For this, PyBlade provides the `@parent` directive:

```html
@block("sidebar")
    @parent

    <p>This content is added to the sidebar.</p>
@endblock
```

`@parent` keeps the parent's content and places the child's content after it.

For example, if the parent contains:

```html
<aside>
    @block("sidebar")
        <p>Default sidebar content.</p>
    @endblock
</aside>
```

the child can keep that content and add more:

```html
@block("sidebar")
    @parent

    <p>This content comes from the child template.</p>
@endblock
```

### The default `slot`

Not all content in a child template needs to be inside a `@block` directive.

As we saw in [Components - Slots](components#slots), PyBlade uses `slot` as the default, unnamed slot. Template inheritance follows the same behavior: any content in the child template that is not inside a `@block` is automatically collected into the default `slot`.

For example:

```html title="templates/welcome.html"
@extends("layouts.base")

<h1>Welcome to my page!</h1>
<p>Content on this page is not inside a block.</p>
```

The parent layout can render this content using:

```html
<main>
    {{ slot }}
</main>
```

This provides a convenient way to pass the main content of a child template to its layout without creating a named block for it.

> **Warning**
>
> The `slot` variable is **not escaped by default** because it is intended to contain rendered HTML. Only use slots with trusted or properly sanitized content. Passing untrusted user input directly into a slot can introduce **cross-site scripting (XSS)** vulnerabilities.

### Named slots

Named slots work the same way in template inheritance as they do in components.

When a child template needs to provide a specific piece of content to the layout, you can define a named slot using `<pb-slot>`:

```html
<pb-slot name="title">Home</pb-slot>
```

The parent layout can then access the slot using its name:

```html
<title>My App - {{ title }}</title>
```

You can define as many named slots as your layout requires. The same `<pb-slot>` syntax and slot behavior used with components also apply here.


---

# Live Components: Introduction

URL: https://docs.pyblade.com/live-components/introduction

Live components allow you  to build dynamic, interactive interfaces using Python and PyBlade templates, without having to write JavaScript for every interaction.

Instead of manually connecting your user interface to JavaScript code, you define a Python component that contains your data and behavior, then use a PyBlade template to describe what it should look like.

PyBlade takes care of the communication between the component and the page, so when the component's state changes, the interface can react accordingly.

This gives you a simple way to build interactive features while keeping your application logic close to the Python code that controls it.

## What is a Live Component?

A Live Component is a special kind of PyBlade component that can **respond to user interactions**.

A regular component is mainly used to display content. A Live Component goes one step further: it can perform an action when the user interacts with it and update its content without requiring you to manually write JavaScript.

For example, a Live Component can be used to build:

* A counter that changes when a button is clicked.
* A search field that updates results as the user types.
* A form that can be validated in real-time and submitted without writing custom JavaScript.
* A list that can be filtered or sorted by the user.
* A dropdown or other interactive UI element.

The logic behind these interactions is written in **Python**, while the interface is defined in a **PyBlade template**, which is just an HTML file where you can use the PyBlade syntax and features you're already familiar with.

## Why use Live Components?

Building an interactive page traditionally means writing JavaScript to listen for user interactions, send AJAX requests to the server, process the response, and update the page.

For simple interactions, this can quickly become more code than the actual feature requires.

Live Components let PyBlade handle this communication for you.

You describe what should happen in your Python component, and PyBlade takes care of communicating with the server and updating the corresponding part of the page.

This allows you to build dynamic interfaces while keeping your application logic in Python, the programming language you already know and love.

## Live Components vs. regular PyBlade components

A regular PyBlade component is primarily a reusable piece of your interface.

For example, you might create a `button`, `card`, or `alert` component and pass data to it when rendering the page.

A Live Component is also a reusable piece of your interface, but it can **perform actions and react to user interactions**.

Think of it this way:

| Regular component                                  | Live Component                              |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Displays content                                   | Displays content and reacts to interactions |
| Mainly receives data                               | Can perform actions                         |
| Used for reusable UI                               | Used for interactive UI                     |
| Does not need server communication after rendering | Can communicate with the server when needed |

So, you don't need to turn every PyBlade component into a Live Component. Use a regular component when you simply need to reuse part of your interface, and use a Live Component when that part needs to **do something** in response to the user.

In the next section, we'll build our first Live Component and see how it works.


---

# Live Components: Quick Start

URL: https://docs.pyblade.com/live-components/quickstart

To begin your journey with Live Components, let's build something simple: a **counter**.

This is a great first example because it demonstrates the main idea behind Live Components without introducing too many concepts at once. We'll create a component that displays a number and provides two buttons to increase or decrease it.

By the end of this guide, you'll have a small interactive component running in your browser, and you'll see how PyBlade can make a page come alive with Python.

## Create a Live Component

PyBlade CLI provides a convenient command for generating Live Components.

Run the following command to create a component named `counter`:

```bash
pyblade make:livecomponent counter
```

This command creates the following files in your project:

```files
components
└── counter
    ├── counter.py
    └── counter.html
```

The Python file will contain the component's logic, while the HTML file will contain its interface.

## Write the component class

Open `components/counter/counter.py` and replace its contents with:

```python title="components/counter/counter.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class Counter(LiveComponent):

    count = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1

    def decrement(self):
        self.count -= 1

    def render(self):
        return self.render_template()
```

Let's look at what each part does.

* `count = 0` — Defines a `count` property and gives it an initial value of `0`.
* `increment()` — Increases `count` by `1` each time the method is called.
* `decrement()` — Decreases `count` by `1` each time the method is called.
* `render()` — Tells PyBlade to render the component's template.

The `increment()` and `decrement()` methods are ordinary Python methods. Later, we'll connect them to actions performed by the user in the browser.

For now, the important thing to understand is that the component contains the Python logic, while its template will describe what the user sees.

## Write the component template

Now open `components/counter/counter.html` and replace its contents with:

```html title="components/counter/counter.html"
<div>
    <h1>{{ count }}</h1>

    <button pb:click="decrement">-</button>
    <button pb:click="increment">+</button>
</div>
```

This is a regular PyBlade template, so you can use the same template syntax you've already learned.

The `{{ count }}` expression displays the current value of the `count` property.

The two buttons use the `pb:click` attribute to connect a browser click to a Python method:

* Clicking `-` calls `decrement()`.
* Clicking `+` calls `increment()`.

That's all we need for our counter.

> **Warning**
>
> A Live Component must have **exactly one root element**.
>
> In the example above, the `<div>` is the component's root element, and everything else is inside it.
>
> If PyBlade detects multiple root elements, it will raise an exception. PyBlade and HTML comments do not count as root elements, so you can safely use comments inside your component.

## Configure Live Components

Before rendering a Live Component, your project needs a small amount of framework-specific configuration.

**django:**

If you're using Django, there are two things you need to configure.

First, add `pyblade.live` to `INSTALLED_APPS` in your Django `settings.py`:

```python title="settings.py"
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    # ...

    "pyblade.live",
]
```

Then, include PyBlade Live's URLs in your project's `urls.py`:

```python title="urls.py"
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    # ...

    path("", include("pyblade.live.urls")),
]
```

That's all. Your Django project is now ready to use Live Components.

**flask:**

Coming soon.

## Render the component

We've created our Live Component, but it still needs a page where it can be displayed.

Let's create a simple PyBlade template for our page:

```bash
pyblade make:template index
```

This creates:

```text
templates/index.html
```

Open the file and add:

```html title="templates/index.html"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Counter</title>
</head>

<body>

    <pb-counter /> <!-- [!code highlight] -->

    @pbscripts <!-- [!code highlight] -->

</body>

</html>
```

The `<pb-counter />` tag tells PyBlade to render our `counter` Live Component at that location.

You may also have noticed the `@pbscripts` directive. Live Components need a small amount of JavaScript in the browser to communicate with the server and update the component when the user interacts with it.

You don't need to write or manage that JavaScript yourself. The `@pbscripts` directive simply includes the scripts required by PyBlade Live Components.

## Create the view

Now we need a view that renders our `index.html` template.

Open your `views.py` file and add:

**django:**

```python title="views.py"
from django.shortcuts import render

def index(request):
    return render(request, "index")
```

**flask:**

Coming soon

The `index()` view simply renders the PyBlade template we created above.

## Register a route

Finally, we need to make the page accessible through a URL.

Open your Django application's `urls.py` file and add:

**django:**

```python title="urls.py"
from django.urls import path

from .views import index

urlpatterns = [
    path("homepage/", index),
]
```

**flask:**

Coming soon

> **Warning**
>
> Make sure that `views.py` and `urls.py` are located in the appropriate Django application directory so that the import shown above works correctly.

Now everything is connected.

When a user visits the page's URL, your framework calls the corresponding view and renders `index.html`. PyBlade then processes the template, encounters the `<pb-counter />` tag, and renders our `Counter` Live Component in its place.

## Test it out

Our Live Component is ready!

Start your development server:

```bash
pyblade dev
```

Then open the URL shown in your terminal and navigate to:

```text
/homepage/
```

You should see the counter with its current value and two buttons.

Try clicking the buttons.

The number should change immediately, without a full page reload.

And that's your first Live Component!

You wrote the component's behavior in **Python**, described its interface with a **PyBlade template**, and PyBlade took care of the communication required to make the component interactive.

We've only scratched the surface of what Live Components can do. In the following sections, we'll explore how to build more powerful components, handle user input, work with forms, respond to events, and much more.


---

# Live Components

URL: https://docs.pyblade.com/live-components/live-components

Live Components are reusable UI elements that combine **Python logic** with a **PyBlade template**. Unlike regular PyBlade components, they can respond to user interactions and update their content without requiring a full page reload.

If you already know how PyBlade components work, Live Components should feel familiar. They are rendered using the same component syntax you have already seen. The main difference is what happens behind the scenes when PyBlade finds the component.

> **Note: PyBlade Components vs. Live Components**
>
> Regular PyBlade components are reusable pieces of HTML that are rendered when the page is generated.
>
> Live Components can do everything regular components can do, but they can also respond to interactions and update themselves dynamically without requiring a full page reload.
>
> In simple terms:
>
> * Regular component: reusable UI.
> * Live Component: reusable UI + Python behavior + live updates.

## Creating a Live Component

A Live Component consists of two parts:

* A **Python class** that inherits from `LiveComponent` and contains the component's logic.
* A **PyBlade template** that defines what the component looks like.

PyBlade CLI provides a command to generate both files for you:

```bash
pyblade make:livecomponent TodoList
```

You can also use *kebab-case* names:

```bash
pyblade make:livecomponent todo-list
```
Or even *snake_case*:

```bash
pyblade make:livecomponent todo_list
```

By default, PyBlade creates the component inside its own folder:

```files
components
└── todo_list
    ├── todo_list.py
    └── todo_list.html
```

The Python file contains the Live Component class:

```python title="components/todo_list/todo_list.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class TodoList(LiveComponent):

    def render(self):
        return self.render_template(context={})
```

And the HTML file contains its PyBlade template:

```html title="components/todo_list/todo_list.html"
<div>
    {# Your component content goes here #}
</div>
```

You can also create these files manually if you prefer.

> **Note: Naming convention**
>
> Generated files and folders use *snake_case*, while component classes use *PascalCase*.
>
> For example, a component named `TodoList` is generated as `todo_list`, while its Python class remains `TodoList`.

## Understanding component folders

You may notice that the Python class and template are placed inside a folder with the same name as the component.

This folder is only there to keep the component's files organized. It is not part of the component's name.

For example:

```files
components
└── todo_list
    ├── todo_list.py
    └── todo_list.html
```

The component is still simply called `todo-list`.

You therefore render it as:

```html
<pb-todo-list />
```

You do not need to include the folder name when rendering the component.

This organization is intentionally abstract. PyBlade uses the folder to keep the component's files together, while the component itself is identified by its name.

### Flat components

If you prefer not to create a separate folder for every Live Component, you can use the `--flat` option:

```bash
pyblade make:livecomponent TodoList --flat
```

The generated files will then be placed directly inside the components directory:

```files
components
├── todo_list.py
├── todo_list.html
└── ...
```

You can also configure this behavior in your `pyblade.toml` file, so you don't have to specify `--flat` every time.

This is simply an organizational choice. It does not change how you render the component.

## Inline components

If a component is small enough, you can keep its template directly inside the Python class instead of creating a separate HTML file.

These are called **inline components**.

For example:

```python title="components/todo_list/todo_list.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class TodoList(LiveComponent):

    def render(self):
        return self.render_inline("""
            <div>
                {# Your content goes here #}
            </div>
        """)
```

You can generate an inline component using the `--inline` option:

```bash
pyblade make:livecomponent TodoList --inline
```

An inline component still requires its Python class. Only the separate template file is omitted.

## Omitting the `render` method

If your component follows PyBlade's conventional naming structure, you can omit the `render` method entirely.

PyBlade Live will automatically use the template associated with the component:

```python title="components/todo_list/todo_list.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class TodoList(LiveComponent):
    ...
```

With the conventional structure:

```files
components
└── todo_list
    ├── todo_list.py
    └── todo_list.html
```

PyBlade automatically knows that `todo_list.html` belongs to the `TodoList` component.

If you use a different template name or location, you can customize the template resolution. For a fixed template, override the `template_name` property with the template path:

```python
class TodoList(LiveComponent):
    template_name = "path.to.template"
```

For more advanced or dynamic template resolution, you can instead override the `get_template_name()` method.

```python
class TodoList(LiveComponent):

    def get_template_name(self):
        return "path.to.template"
```

This lets you keep simple components concise while still giving you full control over which template a component renders.

## Rendering Live Components

Live Components use the **same syntax as regular PyBlade components**.

The preferred way to render the `TodoList` component is with a component tag:

```html
<pb-todo-list />
```

You can also use the `@component` directive:

```html
@component("todo-list")
```

Both forms refer to the same component.

The tag syntax is generally easier to read when your component is part of the HTML structure, while the `@component` directive can be useful when you need to render a component dynamically or use it in a template expression.

> **Note: The same syntax is used for regular and Live Components**
>
> You don't need a special syntax to tell PyBlade that a component is live.
> PyBlade determines which type of component to render when it searches for the component.

### How PyBlade finds a component

Because regular and Live Components use the same syntax, you may wonder how PyBlade knows which one to render.

When PyBlade encounters a component such as:

```html
<pb-card />
```

it searches for a **Live Component first**.

In this case, PyBlade looks for the Python class that defines the `card` Live Component. If it finds it, PyBlade renders the Live Component.

If no Live Component is found, PyBlade then searches for a regular PyBlade component named `card`.

If neither a Live Component nor a regular component can be found, PyBlade raises the `ComponentNotFound` exception indicating that the component could not be resolved.

The process can be summarized as:

```text
<pb-card />
     │
     ▼
Look for a Live Component
     │
     ├── Found ──► Render Live Component
     │
     └── Not found
             │
             ▼
      Look for regular component
             │
             ├── Found ──► Render regular component
             │
             └── Not found ──► Raise an exception
```

This behavior allows you to use the same component syntax throughout your templates without having to remember whether a component is regular or live.

> **Note: Component names must be unique within a component directory.**
>
> You cannot have two regular components with the same name, two Live Components with the same name, or a regular component and a Live Component with the same name in the same directory.
>
> PyBlade also enforces this rule when generating components. If the generated file names would conflict with an existing component, the command returns an error instead of overwriting the existing files.
>
> Components with the same name can only coexist when they are placed in separate component directories.

### Component names

Component tags use the component's **kebab-case name**:

```html
<pb-todo-list />
```

For a Python class named:

```python
class TodoList(LiveComponent):
    ...
```

the corresponding component name is `todo-list`.

You can also use the `@component` directive with the same name:

```html
@component("todo-list")
```

Do not use the Python class name directly in the component tag:

```html
<pb-TodoList />
```

Component names should use **kebab-case** or the supported **snake_case** form.

## Passing data to components

Live Components can receive initial data from the template when they are rendered.

You can pass a value using a regular attribute:

```html
<pb-todo-list title="My Tasks" />
```

If you need to pass a Python value or variable, use a bound attribute by prefixing the attribute name with `:` like this:

```html
<pb-todo-list :title="initial_title" />
```

When using the `@component` directive, you can pass a dictionary containing the data as the second argument:

```html
@component("todo-list", {"title": initial_title})
```

The values in the dictionary are passed to the Live Component in the same way as values passed through a component tag.

> **Note: Already familiar?**
>
> If you have already read the [Passing data to components](/components#passing-data-to-components) section for regular PyBlade components, the syntax here works in the same way.
>
> The difference is what the Live Component does with the received data.

### Receiving data in the component

Data passed to a Live Component is received through its `mount()` method.

The `mount()` method is the Live Component equivalent of Python's `__init__()` method. It is used to receive and/or initialize the data passed to the component when it is created.

For example:

```python title="components/todo_list/todo_list.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class TodoList(LiveComponent):

    def mount(self, title: str):
        self.title = title

    def render(self):
        return self.render_template(context={})
```

When the component is rendered as:

```html
<pb-todo-list title="My Tasks" />
```

PyBlade calls `mount()` during the component's initial creation and passes `"My Tasks"` as the `title` argument.

You can think of `mount()` as the place where you prepare a Live Component when it is first created. It is similar in purpose to a Python class constructor, although it follows the Live Component lifecycle rather than replacing `__init__()`.

We will explore `mount()` and the other lifecycle hooks in the [Lifecycle hooks](lifecycle-hooks) section.

### Automatically assigning component properties

For simple cases, you can omit `mount()` entirely.

If you explicitly declare a typed property whose name matches a value passed to the component, PyBlade Live can assign the value automatically:

```python title="components/todo_list/todo_list.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class TodoList(LiveComponent):

    title: str

    def render(self):
        return self.render_template(context={})
```

You can then render the component as:

```html
<pb-todo-list title="My Tasks" />
```

PyBlade will automatically assign the value to the `title` property.

This is equivalent to assigning the property yourself inside `mount()` for this simple case.

## Rendering components in loops

When rendering elements inside a loop in a Live Component template, PyBlade needs a way to distinguish one item from another when the list changes.

For this reason, elements rendered by a loop should have a **unique `key`**.

For example:

```html title="components/todo_list/todo_list.html"
<div>
    @for (task in tasks)
        <div key="{{ task.id }}">
            {# ... #}
        </div>
    @endfor
</div>
```

The `key` should uniquely identify each item. Using the item's database ID is often a good choice.

The same principle applies when rendering Live Components inside a loop.

You can pass the key directly to a component tag:

```html title="templates/todo.html"
<div>
    @for (task in tasks)
        <pb-task-item :task="task" :key="task.id" />
    @endfor
</div>
```

When using the `@component` directive, the key can be provided as a separate argument:

```html title="templates/todo.html"
<div>
    @for (task in tasks)
        @component(
            "task-item",
            {"task": task},
            key=task.id
        )
    @endfor
</div>
```

> **Note: Why do I need a key?**
>
> When a list changes, PyBlade Live needs to know which rendered element corresponds to which item.
>
> A unique `key` gives each item an identity, allowing PyBlade to correctly match the existing elements with the new ones.
>
> You will see this become especially important when building lists that can be added to, removed from, filtered, or reordered.

{/* ## Including custom JavaScript

> **Danger: 404: Not found**
>
> Coming soon!
## Full-page components

A full-page component allows a Live Component to be assigned directly to a route instead of being rendered inside another PyBlade template.

This is particularly useful when an entire page naturally belongs to a single Live Component, such as a dashboard, task list, profile page, or form.

Full-page components also work especially well with PyBlade's SPA-style navigation using `pb:navigate`, allowing users to move between full-page components without a complete browser page reload.

### Defining a full-page component

Full-page components can be assigned directly to a route using `as_view()`.

**django:**

```python title="urls.py"
from django.urls import path

from components.todo_list import TodoList

urlpatterns = [
    path("tasks/", TodoList.as_view()),
]
```

**flask:**

```python title="app.py"
from flask import Flask

from components.todo_list import TodoList

app = Flask(__name__)

app.add_url_rule(
    "/tasks/",
    view_func=TodoList.as_view(),
)
```

When the user visits `/tasks/`, the `TodoList` component is rendered as the page itself rather than being placed inside another PyBlade template.

### The application layout

Full-page components rendered through routes use your application's layout by default.

PyBlade looks for an application layout at:

```text
templates/
└── layouts/
    └── app.html
```

If this file does not exist, you can generate it with:

```bash
pyblade make:layout app
```

Your application layout should contain a `{{ slot }}` placeholder where the full-page component's content will be rendered:

```html title="templates/layouts/app.html"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="@lang">
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">

    <title>{{ title }}</title>
    
    @pbstyles
    @stack('styles')
</head>

<body>
    {{ slot }}

    @pbscripts
    @stack('scripts')
</body>
</html>
```

The layout is responsible for the common structure of your application, while the full-page component provides the content for the current page. The two `@stack` directives are where components send the stylesheets and scripts they need: see [Scripts and styles](#scripts-and-styles).

You can customize the default application layout in your `pyblade.toml` file. This is useful when your application has a different layout structure, for example:

```toml
[live_component]
layout = "layouts.page"
```

With this configuration, full-page components will use `templates/layouts/page.html` instead of `templates/layouts/app.html`.

### Component-specific layouts

Sometimes a particular full-page component needs a different layout from the application's default layout. For example, a dashboard may use a different navigation structure from a public-facing page.

You can specify a layout directly on the component by overriding its `layout` property:

```python
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class Dashboard(LiveComponent):
    layout = "layouts.dashboard"
```

The `Dashboard` component will then use `templates/layouts/dashboard.html` instead of the default application layout.

You can also use the `@layout` decorator:

```python
from pyblade import LiveComponent
from pyblade.decorators import layout

@layout("layouts.dashboard")
class Dashboard(LiveComponent):
    ...
```

For more advanced cases, you can override the `get_layout()` method to determine the layout dynamically:

```python
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class Dashboard(LiveComponent):

    def get_layout(self):
        if self.user.is_admin:
            return "layouts.admin"

        return "layouts.dashboard"
```

### Navigating between full-page components

Full-page components are especially useful when combined with the `pb:navigate` attribute.

For example, your application layout might contain:

```html
<nav>
    <a href="/tasks/" pb:navigate>Tasks</a>
    <a href="/profile/" pb:navigate>Profile</a>
    <a href="/settings/" pb:navigate>Settings</a>
</nav>

@pbscripts
```

When a user clicks one of these links, PyBlade intercepts the navigation and loads the destination page without performing a full browser reload.

Behind the scenes, PyBlade requests the destination URL, processes the response, and updates the appropriate part of the current page while keeping the application layout in place. A progress bar is displayed during the navigation to provide visual feedback.

The browser URL and history are also updated, so the navigation behaves like normal browser navigation. Users can still use the Back and Forward buttons as expected.

### Page metadata

SPA-style navigation does not prevent each page from having its own metadata.

When navigating to a new page with `pb:navigate`, PyBlade updates the page title to the destination page's `<title>`, and adds the stylesheets and scripts of its `<head>` that the current page doesn't have yet. Other `<meta>` elements are left as they were on the first page loaded.

Every page is still a server-rendered URL: loading it directly, or letting a search engine crawl it, gives the complete page with its own metadata. This keeps full-page components suitable for SEO-friendly applications.

### Accessing route parameters

Full-page components can also receive parameters from the URL.

For example:

**django:**

```python title="urls.py"
urlpatterns = [
    path("tasks/<int:id>/", TaskDetail.as_view()),
]
```

**flask:**

```python name="routes.py"
app.add_url_rule(
    "/tasks/<int:id>/",
    view_func=TaskDetail.as_view(),
)
```

The `id` parameter can then be received by the component's `mount()` method:

```python title="components/task_detail/task_detail.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent
from app.models import Task

class TaskDetail(LiveComponent):

    def mount(self, id: int):
        self.task = Task.objects.get(id=id)

    def render(self):
        return self.render_template()
```

If the user visits `/tasks/1/`, the value `1` is passed to the component as the `id` parameter.

This makes full-page components convenient for pages that depend on route parameters, such as `/tasks/<id>/`, `/users/<id>/`, or `/products/<slug>/`.

## Scripts and styles

A component often needs more than its markup: a library loaded on the page, a stylesheet, or a few lines of JavaScript of its own. PyBlade gives you two directives for that. `@push` sends markup to a place in the layout, and `@script` runs JavaScript that belongs to the component.

### Pushing to the layout

Some markup is needed by a component but belongs elsewhere on the page. A chart component needs its charting library loaded, yet the `<script>` tag should be at the end of the `<body>`, not in the middle of the component.

The layout names those places with `@stack`, as in the [application layout](#the-application-layout) above:

```html title="templates/layouts/app.html"
<head>
    @pbstyles
    @stack('styles') <!-- [!code highlight] -->
</head>

<body>
    {{ slot }}

    @pbscripts
    @stack('scripts') <!-- [!code highlight] -->
</body>
```

A component then sends markup to a stack with `@push` and `@endpush`:

```html title="components/sales_chart.html"
<div>
    <canvas></canvas>
</div>

@push('scripts')
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js"></script>
@endpush
```

When the page is rendered, the `<script>` tag comes out where `@stack('scripts')` is, at the end of the `<body>`. Pushed content comes out in the order it was pushed, so push a library before the code that uses it.

You can push from any template rendered on the page: the page itself, a partial brought in with `@include`, a regular component or a live component, however deeply nested. A push inside an `@if` whose condition is false is not made, and content pushed to a stack the layout doesn't have goes nowhere. The name of a stack may be any expression: `@stack(name)` and `@push(name)` work with a variable too.

A `@push` block may be written after the component's root element, as above. Its content is rendered in the stack, not in the component, so it doesn't count against the single root element a component must have.

#### Pushed content is kept once

The same content is never added to a stack twice. If the `sales_chart` component above is used three times on a page, Chart.js is still loaded **once**:

```html
<pb-sales-chart />
<pb-sales-chart />
<pb-sales-chart />
```

Two pushes count as the same when their rendered content is the same, ignoring the whitespace around it.

> **Note: Coming from Laravel?**
>
> PyBlade's `@push` behaves like Laravel's `@pushOnce`. There is no separate `@pushOnce` directive: loading the same script twice on a page is almost never what you want.

#### Pushing after an action

A live component can also push when it renders again after an action. Say a component only shows a map once the user asks for it:

```python title="components/store_locator/store_locator.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class StoreLocator(LiveComponent):
    map_shown: bool = False

    def show_map(self):
        self.map_shown = True
```

```html title="components/store_locator/store_locator.html"
<div>
    <button pb:click="show_map">Show the map</button>

    @if(map_shown)
        <div id="map"></div>

        @push('scripts')
        <script src="/static/js/maps.js"></script>
        @endpush
    @endif
</div>
```

The component is rendered again without the layout around it, so there is no stack for the script to land in. PyBlade sends what the component pushed along with its new markup, and adds to the page's `scripts` stack whatever the page doesn't hold yet. The script is added once and runs, however many times the button is clicked.

Pushes also follow the user across pages: see [Navigation](/live-components/features/navigation#pushed-content).

### Running JavaScript with `@script`

A plain `<script>` tag inside a live component is rendered like the rest of its markup, but the browser only runs it when the page loads. When the component updates after an action, the new markup is put in place without running any script in it, and the script has no way to reach its component.

Write the component's JavaScript between `@script` and `@endscript` instead, usually after the root element:

```python title="components/counter/counter.py"
from pyblade import LiveComponent

class Counter(LiveComponent):
    count: int = 0

    def increment(self):
        self.count += 1
```

```html title="components/counter/counter.html"
<div>
    <h1>{{ count }}</h1>
    <button pb:click="increment">+</button>
</div>

@script
<script>
    $pb.$watch('count', (now, before) => {
        console.log(`The count went from ${before} to ${now}`);
    });
</script>
@endscript
```

Inside the script, `$pb` is the component: here, the script asks to be told whenever `count` changes. A `@script` written after the root element is moved inside it when the component renders, so it still belongs to the component.

#### When a script runs

A `@script` runs **once each time its component comes onto the page**:

- when the page is loaded,
- when the user navigates to a page with the component, using `pb:navigate`,
- when a [lazy](/live-components/features/lazy-loading) component finishes loading,
- when a parent component's update brings the component in.

It does **not** run again when the component updates, so a script that sets up a listener or a chart does so once.

A `@script` written inside an `@if` runs the first time its markup comes onto the page:

```html
<div>
    <button pb:click="show_chart">Show the chart</button>

    @if(chart_shown)
        <canvas></canvas>

        @script
        <script>
            new Chart($pb.$el.querySelector('canvas'), { type: 'bar', data: {...} });
        </script>
        @endscript
    @endif
</div>
```

Values written with `{{ }}` inside a script are rendered like anywhere else in the template, and a script that has run doesn't run again because such a value changed. The code runs inside an `async` function, so you may use `await` directly.

To load a library a script needs, [push it to a stack](#pushing-to-the-layout) next to the script rather than writing a `<script src>` in the component: it is then loaded once per page, however many components need it.

### The `$pb` object

`$pb` is the component a script belongs to, what `$wire` is to Livewire. It reads and sets the component's properties and calls its actions:

```js
$pb.count           // what "count" holds
$pb.count = 5       // set it, sent with the next request
$pb.increment()     // call an action
await $pb.save()    // ...and wait for the server's answer
```

| | |
|---|---|
| `$pb.name` | What the property `name` holds |
| `$pb.name = value` | Set a property, sent with the next request |
| `$pb.action(...args)` | Call an action |
| `$pb.$get(name)` | What a property holds |
| `$pb.$set(name, value)` | Set a property and send it now |
| `$pb.$call(name, ...args)` | Call an action by name |
| `$pb.$refresh()` | Render the component again |
| `$pb.$el` | The component's root element |
| `$pb.$id` | The component's id |
| `$pb.$emit(event, data)` | Emit an event from the component |
| `$pb.$dispatch(event, data)` | The same as `$emit()` |
| `$pb.$on(event, callback)` | Listen for an event, for as long as the component is on the page |
| `$pb.$watch(name, callback)` | Be told when a property changes |

Each is covered where it belongs: [properties](/live-components/properties#accessing-properties-from-javascript), [actions](/live-components/actions#calling-actions-from-javascript) and [events](/live-components/events#using-javascript-to-interact-with-events).

### The `PyBlade` object

`PyBlade` is available to any JavaScript on the page, inside a `@script` or not: it is what `Livewire` is to Livewire. It finds components, each as its `$pb`:

```js
PyBlade.find('pb-43f55389');  // the component of that id
PyBlade.first();              // the first component on the page
PyBlade.all();                // every component on the page
PyBlade.getByName('Counter'); // every Counter component
```

`getByName()` accepts the name of the class, or its full import path when two components share a name. `PyBlade` also emits and listens for [events](/live-components/events#listening-for-events-from-global-javascript), and moves to another page with `PyBlade.navigate('/tasks/')`.


---

# Properties

URL: https://docs.pyblade.com/live-components/properties

Live components have properties that store data and can be easily accessed within the component's class and template. Properties are defined as attributes on component classes and can be accessed and modified on both the server and client-side. 

This section discusses the basics of adding a property to a component and using it in your application.

## Initializing properties

In a standard Python class, to initialize properties or attributes, we use the `__init__()` dunder method. However, in a PyBlade Live component's class, you can set initial values for properties within your component's `mount()` method.

```python
from pyblade import LiveComponent
from app.models import Task

class TodoList(LiveComponent):

    def mount(self):
        self.tasks = Task.objects.all()
```

In this example, when the component renders for the first time, all the existing tasks in the database are made available through the `tasks` variable.
